slides.title: S3 starts with an object, a key and an access pattern
copy: Object storage
A bucket holds objects identified by keys. Objects combine data, metadata and a storage class; key prefixes organize names rather than create normal filesystem directories.
Good fits
Static assets, backups and data lakes fit object access patterns. Many tiny objects can amplify request and metadata overhead; model the full cost.
Choose the right interface
Object APIs differ from POSIX files and block devices. They do not provide general POSIX locking or database-style in-place updates. Match latency, update and query needs to the right interface.
Remember: Choose storage semantics first, then the service and storage class.
slides.layout: Three rich conceptual teaching stations with glossy object/service illustrations and readable paragraphs.

slides.title: Consistency does not replace coordination
copy: Read the completed write
General-purpose S3 object operations provide strong consistency for successful writes, overwrites, deletes and listings.
Concurrent changes still matter
Two clients can overwrite the same key. Use conditional requests and version-aware application logic when concurrent updates must be controlled.
Durability is a separate property
Durable storage does not prevent an authorized delete or application mistake. Versioning, retention, backups and replication address different risks.
Remember: Consistent reads do not make a multi-object business transaction atomic.
slides.layout: One central glossy metaphor with three surrounding explanation cards.

slides.title: S3 access: identity, resource policy and ownership
copy: Start private
Use Block Public Access and least-privilege identity and bucket policies. An explicit deny overrides an allow.
Understand ownership
Bucket owner enforced Object Ownership disables ACLs and centralizes ownership and policy-based access. Cross-account workflows still need appropriate permissions.
Evaluate the whole request
Check principal, action, object or bucket resource, policy conditions and applicable organization or endpoint controls. KMS access can be required separately.
Remember: AccessDenied is an authorization result; diagnose the specific request and policy boundary.
slides.layout: Asymmetric two-column layout with three numbered teaching areas and compact illustrative examples.

slides.title: Access points and private network access
copy: Give applications scoped entry points
S3 access points provide named endpoints and policies for particular application access patterns. Bucket authorization must support the intended access.
Reach S3 privately
A gateway endpoint provides supported VPC access to S3 through route-table integration. Interface endpoints support different private-connectivity requirements and costs.
Use defense in depth
An endpoint policy constrains access through that endpoint; it does not grant bucket permission or encrypt the data by itself.
Remember: A private network path and permission to access an object are separate controls.
slides.layout: Three rich conceptual teaching stations with glossy object/service illustrations and readable paragraphs.

slides.title: Encryption: protect data and authorize the key
copy: Encryption at rest
Server-side encryption protects stored object data. SSE-S3 and KMS-based options have different key-management, authorization and audit implications.
KMS permissions matter
An S3 permission alone can be insufficient for KMS-encrypted objects. Validate the relevant KMS key policy, IAM permissions and regional key availability.
Protect transport too
Use HTTPS and appropriate bucket-policy conditions. Plan key access for replication, cross-account readers and recovery rather than only the writer.
Remember: Encryption is useful only when authorized applications can use the keys and unauthorized callers cannot.
slides.layout: One central glossy metaphor with three surrounding explanation cards.

slides.title: Versioning preserves object history
copy: Keep distinct versions
Versioning preserves prior versions when a key is overwritten. Deleting without a version ID usually adds a delete marker rather than erasing all history.
Recover deliberately
Recover the required version or remove the appropriate delete marker. Permanently deleting a particular version removes that stored version.
Manage the accumulated cost
Noncurrent versions and delete markers need deliberate lifecycle rules. Suspending versioning is not the same as deleting historical versions.
Remember: Versioning creates recovery options; lifecycle and permissions determine whether they remain useful.
slides.layout: Asymmetric two-column layout with three numbered teaching areas and compact illustrative examples.

slides.title: Object Lock: retention and legal hold
copy: Use version-level protection
Object Lock protects eligible object versions in a versioned bucket. A legal hold is separate from a time-based retention period.
Governance mode
Appropriately authorized callers can bypass governance retention when they explicitly request that operation.
Compliance mode
Protected versions cannot be deleted or have retention shortened before expiry, including by the account root user.
Remember: Choose retention mode, duration and recovery procedures before applying irreversible protection.
slides.layout: Three rich conceptual teaching stations with glossy object/service illustrations and readable paragraphs.

slides.title: Serve private static objects through CloudFront
copy: Separate delivery from storage
S3 stores static objects while CloudFront caches and delivers them closer to users. The application can keep its dynamic compute separately.
Protect the origin
For a supported S3 bucket origin, use Origin Access Control and the appropriate bucket policy to restrict direct origin access.
Choose the endpoint deliberately
An S3 website endpoint and a regular S3 bucket origin have different capabilities. Viewer HTTPS and origin access must match the chosen design.
Remember: A CDN improves delivery; it does not automatically make an exposed bucket private.
slides.layout: One central glossy metaphor with three surrounding explanation cards.

slides.title: Online storage classes: availability and recovery tradeoffs
copy: S3 Standard
Frequent access, multi-AZ resilience and no minimum storage-duration commitment make it a flexible starting point.
Standard-IA
Infrequent access with rapid retrieval across multiple AZs. Account for retrieval charges, minimum duration and minimum billable size.
One Zone-IA
Infrequent-access data in one AZ. Use when the data can be recreated or another recoverable copy exists; it does not tolerate loss of that AZ.
Remember: Durability design, availability, retrieval charges and AZ failure tolerance are different dimensions.
slides.layout: Asymmetric two-column layout with three numbered teaching areas and compact illustrative examples.

slides.title: Glacier classes: choose retrieval behavior
copy: Glacier Instant Retrieval
Archive-oriented storage with immediate access for rarely read objects. Retrieval and minimum-duration charges still matter.
Glacier Flexible Retrieval
Asynchronous restore supports different retrieval tiers. Plan the restoration delay, temporary restored copy and retrieval charges.
Glacier Deep Archive
Long-retention data with a longer recovery lead time. A cheaper stored copy may be unsuitable for a short recovery objective.
Remember: Archive selection must satisfy the time needed to restore usable data, not just the storage price.
slides.layout: Three rich conceptual teaching stations with glossy object/service illustrations and readable paragraphs.

slides.title: Intelligent-Tiering follows changing access
copy: Unknown or changing patterns
Eligible objects enter Frequent Access, then move to Infrequent Access after 30 days without access and Archive Instant Access after 90 days.
Separate online and optional archive tiers
Optional Archive Access starts after at least 90 days without access; Deep Archive Access after at least 180 days. Both require a restore before reading.
Include the overhead
Monitoring and automation charges apply to eligible objects. Objects below 128 KB stay in Frequent Access and are not monitored or charged the monitoring fee.
Remember: Intelligent-Tiering optimizes access-tier placement; it does not decide whether an object should exist.
slides.layout: One central glossy metaphor with three surrounding explanation cards.

slides.title: Lifecycle rules manage the whole object history
copy: Transition with intent
Rules can move eligible objects to supported storage classes or expire them. Filter the intended key prefixes or tags and validate transition constraints.
Distinguish current and noncurrent versions
Current-version expiration, noncurrent-version expiration and expired delete-marker cleanup solve different problems.
Model the complete bill
Minimum storage duration, retrieval charges, small-object minimums and archive metadata overhead can outweigh a lower price per GB.
Remember: A lifecycle rule is an automated data-retention decision; test the scope before applying it.
slides.layout: Asymmetric two-column layout with three numbered teaching areas and compact illustrative examples.

slides.title: Replication: same Region or another Region?
copy: Choose the failure boundary
SRR creates another same-Region copy; CRR creates a copy in another Region. Choose the destination for latency, ownership, compliance and recovery needs.
Prepare both buckets
Enable required versioning, permissions and replication configuration. KMS-encrypted data needs supported key permissions and configuration.
Replication and lifecycle cooperate
Destination retention or storage-class choices can differ from source choices. Check what is replicated rather than assuming every bucket setting is copied.
Remember: A replicated copy is useful only if its permissions, keys and recovery design survive the intended failure.
slides.layout: Three rich conceptual teaching stations with glossy object/service illustrations and readable paragraphs.

slides.title: Replication timing, existing objects and deletion
copy: New versus existing data
Live replication handles eligible new objects after configuration. Existing objects or repair operations can require S3 Batch Replication.
Replication Time Control

S3 RTC applies to eligible live replication, not Batch Replication. Monitor replication delay and failures. Its SLA starts service credits below a 99.9% monthly 15-minute replication percentage, subject to terms.
Protect recovery independence
Delete-marker handling requires deliberate configuration. Permanent version deletion and all source-side operations do not automatically become equivalent destination actions.
Remember: Asynchronous replication has a recovery-point implication and is not a substitute for independent retention.
slides.layout: One central glossy metaphor with three surrounding explanation cards.

slides.title: S3 event notifications: react without coupling
copy: Choose events and filters
Object creation, removal, restore and replication events support different workflows. Native notification filtering uses supported key prefixes and suffixes, not arbitrary wildcard expressions.
Select the destination
Supported direct destinations include Lambda, standard SQS queues and standard SNS topics. Permissions and regional compatibility must be correct.
Design for retries
Delivery usually takes seconds but can take a minute or longer. Events may repeat or arrive out of order. Use idempotent processing and a plan for failures.
Remember: An object event is a signal to process; it is not exactly-once execution.
slides.layout: Asymmetric two-column layout with three numbered teaching areas and compact illustrative examples.

slides.title: EventBridge adds richer event routing
copy: Enable bucket delivery
Configure the bucket to send supported S3 events to EventBridge, then use event patterns to select the work.
Filter actual event fields
Bucket, object key, object size and event type can support routing decisions. Custom object metadata may require a separate lookup.
Use the event platform
Route to supported targets, such as Step Functions or queues. Configure retries, dead-letter handling and optional archive/replay deliberately.
Remember: Richer routing does not remove duplication, permissions or downstream failure handling.
slides.layout: Three rich conceptual teaching stations with glossy object/service illustrations and readable paragraphs.

slides.title: Scale requests across useful key prefixes
copy: Plan for request distribution
The reference baseline is at least 3,500 write-type or 5,500 GET/HEAD requests per second per partitioned prefix. Scaling to a new request pattern can be gradual.
Use parallelism deliberately
Spread independent work and connections across suitable prefixes. Prefixes are parts of keys, not a fixed set of physical folders.
Observe the real bottleneck
Handle transient throttling with retries and backoff. Client capacity, network throughput and KMS request quotas can constrain the complete system.
Remember: High S3 capacity does not guarantee that the client, encryption path or network can keep up.
slides.layout: One central glossy metaphor with three surrounding explanation cards.

slides.title: Multipart upload: parallelize and retry parts
copy: Divide a large object
Initiate to obtain an upload ID, upload numbered parts and retain their ETags, then complete using the required part information.
Retry only what failed
Parallel parts improve throughput; retry a failed part rather than the whole object. Consider multipart around 100 MB; use it beyond the single-PUT limit.
Completion is a separate step
Parts become a completed object only after completion succeeds. Validate checksums; the final ETag is not necessarily an MD5. Use the module reference for current size limits.
Remember: Multipart upload is a managed transfer lifecycle, not just several simultaneous PUT requests.
slides.layout: Asymmetric two-column layout with three numbered teaching areas and compact illustrative examples.

slides.title: Incomplete multipart uploads still consume storage
copy: Recognize stranded work
A failed or abandoned upload can leave billable parts even though no completed object appears in normal object listing.
Inspect deliberately
Use multipart-upload listing operations and inspect the outstanding upload before deciding whether to resume or abort it.
Automate cleanup
A lifecycle rule can abort incomplete multipart uploads after the chosen number of days. This is different from expiring completed objects or noncurrent versions.
Remember: Successful cleanup requires the right lifecycle action, not merely deleting an object key.
slides.layout: Three rich conceptual teaching stations with glossy object/service illustrations and readable paragraphs.

slides.title: Byte-range GET: fetch only the needed bytes
copy: Download independent ranges
A Range request retrieves a selected byte interval. Parallel ranges can accelerate suitable large-object downloads.
Recover smaller failures
Retry a failed range instead of restarting the entire download. Coordinate the assembled output and request concurrency.
Read partial content
Fetch a file header or needed segment without transferring the whole object. Pin the version or use conditions when consistency across requests matters.
Remember: Less transferred data helps only when the application understands and correctly assembles the selected bytes.
slides.layout: One central glossy metaphor with three surrounding explanation cards.

slides.title: Transfer Acceleration helps distant uploads
copy: Use an edge entry point
Eligible accelerated requests enter through an AWS edge location and traverse the AWS network toward the bucket's Region.
Combine with multipart
Parallel multipart transfers and acceleration address different parts of the transfer problem and can be used together.
Measure the benefit
Distance, network path, object size and client behavior affect the result. Benchmark and include acceleration charges rather than assuming every transfer becomes faster.
Remember: Acceleration optimizes the journey to a bucket; it is not multi-Region object replication.
slides.layout: Asymmetric two-column layout with three numbered teaching areas and compact illustrative examples.

slides.title: Legacy Select: reduce data before transfer
copy: Understand the historical idea
S3 Select and Glacier Select used server-side SQL-style filtering to return selected rows and columns rather than a whole supported object.
Why the pattern mattered
Returning a smaller result can reduce network transfer and client-side processing. It is different from a general-purpose database index.
Choose an available query path
S3 Select is unavailable to new customers; existing customers can continue using it. Glacier Select is historical context here. Evaluate Athena or another suitable engine for new analytical designs.
Remember: Filtering one object's content and querying a data lake are different architectural operations.
slides.layout: Three rich conceptual teaching stations with glossy object/service illustrations and readable paragraphs.

slides.title: Storage Class Analysis informs lifecycle decisions
copy: Observe before transitioning
S3 Analytics Storage Class Analysis examines access patterns to help assess Standard-to-Standard-IA transition opportunities.
Know the scope
It is not a universal recommendation engine for One Zone-IA or Glacier classes. Lifecycle execution is a separate configuration.
Use the reports

Initial analysis appears in 24–48 hours and updates daily; recommendations usually need 30 days or more of observations. Export daily CSV reports for spreadsheets or BI tools, including the QuickSight workflow shown in older materials.
Remember: A recommendation informs the decision; a lifecycle rule performs the transition.
slides.layout: One central glossy metaphor with three surrounding explanation cards.

slides.title: Storage Lens: see storage across the organization
copy: Choose the aggregation scope
Analyze supported organization, account, Region, bucket and prefix views to identify growth, cost and protection patterns.
Use the default or a custom dashboard
The default dashboard is preconfigured and can be disabled rather than deleted. Custom dashboards provide a tailored scope.
Export for further analysis
Configure supported daily exports, such as CSV or Parquet, and the appropriate access permissions for the destination.
Remember: Aggregated visibility helps locate problems; it does not apply the corrective policy by itself.
slides.layout: Asymmetric two-column layout with three numbered teaching areas and compact illustrative examples.

slides.title: Storage Lens: summary and cost signals
copy: Measure the footprint
Storage bytes and object counts reveal growing or underused storage. Compare the right account, bucket or prefix over time.
Find hidden retained data
Noncurrent-version bytes and incomplete-multipart-upload bytes can reveal costs that a normal current-object listing misses.
Turn a signal into an action
Investigate the affected data, then choose retention, cleanup or class transitions according to recovery and access requirements.
Remember: Reducing bytes is useful only when it preserves required data and recovery options.
slides.layout: Three rich conceptual teaching stations with glossy object/service illustrations and readable paragraphs.

slides.title: Storage Lens: protection, ownership and event configuration
copy: Protection metrics
Inspect versioning, MFA Delete, encryption-related and cross-Region replication indicators to locate gaps in expected safeguards.
Access-management metrics
Object Ownership indicators show which buckets use ownership configurations such as bucket owner enforced.
Event metrics
Notification-enabled bucket counts help assess where object events are configured. Configuration presence alone does not prove successful downstream processing.
Remember: A configuration metric is evidence of a setting, not proof that every object and workflow is protected.
slides.layout: One central glossy metaphor with three surrounding explanation cards.

slides.title: Storage Lens: activity, performance and status codes
copy: Activity metrics
Request counts, GET, PUT and LIST operations and downloaded bytes show how workloads use stored data.
Performance-related configuration
Transfer Acceleration configuration indicators help locate enabled buckets; measure actual transfer results separately.
Detailed status codes
Success, forbidden and not-found counts reveal different request outcomes. Investigate authorization, object existence and application behavior before changing retention.
Remember: Stored capacity, request activity and request success tell different parts of the operational story.
slides.layout: Asymmetric two-column layout with three numbered teaching areas and compact illustrative examples.

slides.title: Storage Lens: choose the needed metric tier
copy: Free usage visibility
Free daily metrics include storage, cost, protection, ownership, performance and event-configuration signals. Their console query window is 14 days.
Advanced metrics and recommendations
Paid advanced metrics add activity, detailed status and deeper cost/protection insights, recommendations and CloudWatch publishing. Prefix-level metrics are not published to CloudWatch.
Match history to the decision
All metrics are retained for 15 months. Free metrics can be queried for 14 days; advanced metrics for 15 months. Retention and query access are different.
Remember: Pay for the scope and history needed to answer a real operational or cost question.
slides.layout: Three rich conceptual teaching stations with glossy object/service illustrations and readable paragraphs.

slides.title: Build an object-metadata index for application queries
copy: Separate payload from lookup
S3 holds the object; DynamoDB can hold tenant, upload date, category, object size and key for application-specific lookups.
Maintain the index
An event-driven processor can update metadata after object changes. Handle duplicates, out-of-order events and failures, then reconcile missing or stale records.
Design the query keys
Design partition and sort keys for tenant/date and attribute queries. Total bytes per customer needs a reliable aggregate or reconciliation. Enforce tenant access and account for index lag.
Remember: An application index must be maintained and repaired; object storage does not make that workflow atomic.
slides.layout: One central glossy metaphor with three surrounding explanation cards.

slides.title: Keep static delivery separate from dynamic processing
copy: Static path
Store suitable assets as objects and deliver them through an appropriate cache. Keep permission checks aligned with the intended audience.
Dynamic path
Use application compute or APIs for business logic and databases for transactional state. Do not expect a static object to execute server-side application code.
Upload without proxying every byte
An authorized service can issue a bounded presigned upload request. Validate the intended key, method, expiry and application workflow.
Remember: Each layer should own one responsibility: delivery, computation, metadata lookup or durable object storage.
slides.layout: Asymmetric two-column layout with three numbered teaching areas and compact illustrative examples.

slides.title: Choose recovery controls for the actual failure
copy: Accidental overwrite
Version history can restore an earlier object state if the required versions have been retained and permissions allow recovery.
Malicious or mistaken deletion
Retention and legal-hold controls protect eligible versions; independent backup and access boundaries reduce correlated failure.
Regional disruption
A deliberately configured remote replica can support recovery, but data lag, keys, permissions and application dependencies still affect the result.
Remember: Test the full restore path; the existence of another copy does not prove a usable recovery.
slides.layout: Three rich conceptual teaching stations with glossy object/service illustrations and readable paragraphs.

slides.title: S3 architecture decisions: fit the access and failure model
copy: Start with semantics
Choose object, file, block, database or analytical access according to how the application reads, updates and searches data.
Choose the data lifecycle
Match online access or restore delays, retention, replication boundaries and complete storage/retrieval costs.
Validate the complete request path
Include identity, encryption, network reachability, delivery, events, indexes and operational metrics. Check current service limits before implementation.
Remember: A strong S3 design balances access, security, recovery, performance and cost across the whole application.
slides.layout: One central glossy metaphor with three surrounding explanation cards.

slides.title: Static assets: servers, shared files or an object origin?
copy: Local assets on web servers
Serving static files from EC2 keeps the web tier responsible for availability, patching and scaling. Instance store is ephemeral; EBS introduces its own persistence and AZ considerations.
Shared files for a web fleet
EFS can provide a shared Linux file namespace for suitable web applications. The compute fleet and filesystem remain dependencies that need security, performance and resilience planning.
Object-native static delivery
S3 with an appropriate CloudFront origin can deliver suitable static objects without a web-server fleet. Keep dynamic application processing separate where the workload allows.
Remember: Add compute and filesystem layers when their semantics are needed, rather than merely to hold unchanged static objects.
